blocks.label: Practice + teach-it-back
steps: Do 20 practice questions on monitoring (Tutorials Dojo practice exams or Skill Builder topic reviews).
Teach-it-back, out loud with notes closed: why does Model Quality monitoring need ground-truth labels, and where do those labels come from?

keyTerms.def: SageMaker's continuous monitoring for endpoints; compares live traffic against a baseline.
Statistics and constraints computed from training data — the 'normal' production is compared against.
Production input distribution shifts away from training data.
The input-to-label relationship itself changes; harder to catch, needs fresh labels.
Human-verified correct labels, merged with predictions to compute model-quality metrics.
Feature-attribution method; the explainability monitor watches for attribution drift.
Watches a metric and fires an action (e.g., SNS notification) when a threshold is breached.

notes.heading: The four Model Monitor types
points: `Data Quality`: watches for schema changes and statistical drift in incoming features versus the baseline (built on Deequ-style constraints).
`Model Quality`: watches accuracy/precision/recall drift — the only type that needs `ground truth` labels merged with predictions.
`Model Bias`: watches Clarify bias metrics (e.g., disparate impact) drifting outside the baseline's acceptable range.
`Model Explainability`: watches `SHAP` feature-attribution drift — which features the model relies on has changed.
Exam shortcut: three types compare against the baseline alone; only Model Quality needs fresh human-verified labels.

notes.heading: Baselines and schedules
points: A baseline job (`suggest_baseline`) runs over training/validation data and writes statistics plus constraints to S3.
A monitoring schedule runs on a cron expression, analyzes recent production data, and writes violation reports to S3.
Each run also emits CloudWatch metrics, so violations can trigger alarms without anyone reading the S3 reports.
Baselines go stale: re-run the baseline job after retraining, or you will alarm on your own improved model.

notes.heading: Data drift vs concept drift
points: `Data drift`: the input distribution shifted — P(X) changed. Caught by the Data Quality monitor.
`Concept drift`: the inputs look the same but the right answers changed — P(y|X) changed. Shows up in Model Quality, needs fresh labels.
Example: loan applicants' income distribution shifts (data drift) vs. what counts as creditworthy changes after a policy update (concept drift).
The exam often pairs them as a two-option trap — anchor on whether the inputs changed or the relationship changed.

notes.heading: CloudWatch for ML
points: Endpoint metrics live in the `AWS/SageMaker` namespace: `Invocations`, `Invocation4XXErrors`, `Invocation5XXErrors`, `ModelLatency`, `OverheadLatency`.
Alarms watch a metric and fire actions (SNS notification, EventBridge event) when a threshold breaches.
`CloudWatch Logs` captures training-job logs and endpoint container logs — first stop when a job fails.
Dashboards combine metrics, alarms, and log queries into one operational view of an endpoint.

notes.heading: The violation response loop
points: Violation detected → CloudWatch metric → alarm → SNS/EventBridge notification.
Response options: page a human, trigger a retraining pipeline (Day 20), or roll the endpoint back to a previous model version.
The exam's favorite phrasing: `automatically retrain when drift is detected` — that is Model Monitor plus EventBridge plus SageMaker Pipelines.
Monitoring without a response plan is just expensive logging — the loop is the point.

objectives: Explain the four SageMaker Model Monitor types and what drift each one catches
Describe how baselines and monitoring schedules work, and where violations surface
Use CloudWatch metrics, alarms, and logs to observe a SageMaker endpoint in production

quiz.q: Which SageMaker Model Monitor type requires ground-truth labels merged with predictions?
quiz.why: Only model-quality metrics (accuracy, precision, recall) need true labels; the other three compare against the baseline alone.

quiz.q: A monitoring schedule reports that feature distributions match training, but accuracy is steadily falling. What drift is this?
quiz.why: Inputs unchanged but the input-to-label relationship moved — classic concept drift.

options: Live production traffic sampled for one hour
A baseline job run over training/validation data, stored in S3
quiz.q: Where does a Model Monitor baseline come from?
quiz.why: The baseline job computes statistics and constraints from training data; everything later is compared to it.

options: It emails the account root automatically
It emits CloudWatch metrics you alarm on, e.g., routed to SNS
It opens an AWS Support case
quiz.q: Model Monitor finds a violation. How does the on-call team get notified?
quiz.why: Model Monitor publishes metrics and S3 reports; notification is your CloudWatch alarm to SNS or EventBridge wiring.

quiz.q: Which CloudWatch metric best catches an endpoint returning server-side errors to callers?
quiz.why: 5XX means server-side invocation errors — alarm on it for paging.

steps: Do 20 practice questions on MLOps and CI/CD (Tutorials Dojo practice exams or Skill Builder topic reviews).

keyTerms.def: An event or schedule that starts a new training run.
Managed ML workflow orchestration with steps for processing, training, evaluation, and registration.
Versioned catalog of candidate models with metrics, lineage, and approval status.
Manual Approved/Rejected checkpoint a model must pass before it can deploy.
Event bus that routes Model Monitor violations into pipeline executions.
Human review workflows for low-confidence ML predictions in production.
Human-verified labels flowing back into evaluation, monitoring, and retraining.

notes.heading: Retraining triggers
points: `Scheduled`: retrain on a cadence (weekly, monthly) as fresh data accumulates — simplest, most common.
`Drift/violation-driven`: a Model Monitor violation fires an EventBridge event that starts the pipeline.
`New-data-driven`: retrain when enough new labeled data lands in S3 to matter.
`Performance-degradation`: a business or model-quality metric slips below its target.
Exam phrasing to recognize: `automatically retrain when data drift is detected`.

notes.heading: SageMaker Pipelines
points: A pipeline is a DAG of steps: processing (feature prep), training, evaluation, condition check, register model, optionally deploy.
Pipelines are defined in the SDK, versioned, and re-runnable — they separate experiment code from production orchestration.
The evaluation step can gate registration: only register the model if metrics beat the current production version.
Retraining is just re-executing the pipeline with fresh data — same code, new inputs.

notes.heading: Model Registry and approval gates
points: The registry versions every candidate model with its metrics, artifacts, and lineage.
Approval status moves `PendingManualApproval` to `Approved` or `Rejected` — a human decision.
CI/CD deploys only `Approved` versions, which stops a bad automatic retrain from ever reaching production.
This is the exam's answer whenever a question wants automation with a human safety check on deployment.

notes.heading: CodePipeline for ML
points: CodePipeline orchestrates the outer loop: source change (code or config) to build/test to pipeline execution to deploy.
EventBridge wires monitor violations into pipeline starts, closing the Day 19 loop.
Keep the layers straight: CodePipeline orchestrates releases; SageMaker Pipelines orchestrates ML workflows.

notes.heading: A2I: human-in-the-loop
points: `A2I` (Augmented AI) routes low-confidence predictions to human reviewers — a private workforce, a vendor team, or Mechanical Turk.
Humans verify or correct the prediction; the verified labels land in S3.
Those labels become ground truth for evaluation, for Day 19-style model-quality monitoring, and for retraining.
Reach for A2I when errors are costly: content moderation, document extraction review, anything where a wrong prediction has consequences.
Do not confuse with Ground Truth: Ground Truth labels raw data for training; A2I reviews live predictions in production.

objectives: List the four standard retraining triggers and match each to a detection mechanism

quiz.q: A Model Monitor data-quality violation should automatically start retraining. Which service routes the violation event to the pipeline?
quiz.why: EventBridge consumes the monitor's events and triggers the SageMaker Pipeline execution.

quiz.q: Where does the human checkpoint live in SageMaker MLOps?
quiz.why: Registry versions sit at PendingManualApproval until a human marks them Approved — only then can CI/CD deploy.

quiz.q: Which is NOT a standard retraining trigger?
quiz.why: IAM changes affect permissions, not model freshness; the other three are the classic triggers.

options: Training data needs labeling at scale from scratch
Low-confidence predictions need human verification before acting
quiz.q: A2I is the right choice when…
quiz.why: A2I is human-in-the-loop review of live predictions, not a labeling service (that is Ground Truth) or infrastructure.

options: Ground truth for evaluation, monitoring, and retraining
quiz.q: Verified A2I labels are stored in S3 and then used for…
quiz.why: Human-verified labels close the loop — they become the ground truth that model-quality monitoring needs.

keyTerms.def: IAM role that SageMaker assumes to act on your behalf in jobs and endpoints.
The policy stating who is allowed to assume a role, e.g., the SageMaker service principal.
Granting only the actions on only the resources a workload needs — nothing more.

Free, S3- and DynamoDB-specific VPC endpoint type.

Audit log of AWS API activity: who did what, to which resource, and when.

notes.heading: SageMaker execution roles
points: An execution role is an IAM role that SageMaker assumes on your behalf for training jobs, endpoints, and notebook instances.
The `trust policy` lets the `sagemaker.amazonaws.com` service principal assume the role.
The `permissions policy` grants exactly the S3, ECR, CloudWatch Logs, KMS, and VPC actions the workload needs.
Never embed long-lived user access keys in training code — the role provides temporary, scoped credentials instead.

notes.heading: Least privilege in practice
points: Scope S3 permissions to the specific data and model buckets, not `s3:*`.
Use separate roles for training, inference, and notebooks — a compromised notebook should not be able to retrain models.
Permission boundaries let delegated admins create roles without exceeding a maximum privilege ceiling.

notes.heading: KMS: encryption at rest
points: `SSE-S3`: S3 encrypts with AWS-managed keys — simple, but you do not control the key.
`SSE-KMS`: S3 encrypts with a KMS key you manage — required when the organization must control or audit key usage.
SageMaker training volumes and model artifacts can be encrypted with your KMS key via `VolumeKmsKeyId` and related settings.
`Key policies` are resource-based: they decide who may use versus administer each key.

notes.heading: Encryption in transit
points: Endpoint invocations, console access, and API calls use TLS by default.
A bucket policy with `aws:SecureTransport` set to false and effect `Deny` blocks any non-HTTPS S3 access.
Exam pattern: `all traffic must be encrypted in transit` is almost always this condition.

notes.heading: S3 bucket policies that show up on exams
points: Bucket policies are `resource-based` JSON attached to the bucket itself.
Pattern 1: deny `s3:PutObject` when `s3:x-amz-server-side-encryption` is not `aws:kms` — enforces KMS encryption on upload.
Pattern 2: deny all actions when `aws:SecureTransport` is false — enforces TLS.
Pattern 3: restrict access to a VPC endpoint via `aws:sourceVpce` — keeps bucket traffic private (see Day 21).

notes.heading: SageMaker in a VPC
points: Attach training jobs, endpoints, and notebook instances to private subnets plus security groups via the VPC config.
They get elastic network interfaces in your VPC and no public IPs.
By default there is no internet route — outbound internet requires a NAT gateway in the design.
Security groups control which ports and peers each resource can talk to.

notes.heading: Network isolation
points: `EnableNetworkIsolation=True` gives training containers zero network access — no internet, no AWS API calls.
The SageMaker platform still stages input data onto the instance, so training on S3 data keeps working.
Use it for the strictest data-governance requirements, where even the training code must not exfiltrate.
Exam signal: `containers must not access the network` or `no internet access under any circumstance`.

notes.heading: PrivateLink and VPC endpoints
points: `Interface endpoints` (PrivateLink) keep traffic to AWS services — SageMaker API, SageMaker Runtime — off the public internet.
The `gateway endpoint` for S3 is free and is the exam's standard answer for private S3 access from a VPC.
Exam signal: `access AWS services without traversing the internet` points at VPC endpoints, not NAT.
Endpoints have their own policies, so you can further restrict which actions flow through them.

notes.heading: NAT gateway
points: A NAT gateway lets private-subnet resources initiate outbound internet (package installs, external APIs) with no inbound exposure.
It bills hourly plus per gigabyte processed — the exam's cost questions bring it up for a reason.
If the workload only needs AWS services, prefer VPC endpoints over NAT: private and cheaper.
Exam signal: `private subnet needs outbound internet only`.

notes.heading: CloudTrail auditing
points: CloudTrail records AWS API calls: identity, action, resource, timestamp, and source IP.
Trails deliver log files to S3; `log file validation` proves the logs were not tampered with.
A multi-region trail captures activity in every region from one place.
Answers the exam's favorite audit question: `who changed the endpoint configuration, and when?`

objectives: Choose an evaluation approach for FM and RAG systems: automatic metrics, human review, or a judge model
Monitor FMs and agents with CloudWatch metrics, invocation logs, and traces, and diagnose common agent failures
Reduce FM inference, embedding, and vector storage cost
Configure Bedrock Guardrails and pick the right credential type for FM access
Scan pipeline code and container images for vulnerabilities

blocks.label: Warm-up
steps: Clear your bounty board and due flashcards — today ends with the Chapter 4 boss
From memory: which Day 11 metrics apply to generated text, and what does each one measure?

Skim [Domain 4 in the exam guide](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/aws-certification/latest/machine-learning-engineer-associate-02/machine-learning-engineer-associate-02-domain4.html) and mark 4.1.5–4.1.6, 4.2.7–4.2.10, 4.3.1 and 4.3.8–4.3.9 — all new in MLA-C02

blocks.label: New material
steps: 📖 Read first: [Bedrock evaluations](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/evaluation.html) · [Guardrails](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/guardrails.html) · [monitoring Bedrock](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/monitoring.html)

Text metrics: `BLEU` scores n-gram precision against a reference (translation); `ROUGE` scores n-gram recall (summarization); `BERTScore` compares meaning using embeddings, so paraphrases still score well

Bedrock evaluation job types: automatic (built-in metrics such as accuracy, robustness, toxicity), human (your own team or an AWS-managed workforce), and `LLM-as-a-judge` (a second model scores correctness, completeness, faithfulness, and harmfulness)

RAG evaluation splits in two: retrieval quality (context relevance, context coverage) and generation quality (correctness, faithfulness to the retrieved context, citation accuracy). Fix whichever half is failing

FM monitoring: CloudWatch `AWS/Bedrock` metrics — `Invocations`, `InvocationLatency`, `InputTokenCount`, `OutputTokenCount`, `InvocationThrottles`. `Model invocation logging` (off by default) sends full prompts and responses to CloudWatch Logs or S3; CloudTrail records who called which API

Agent monitoring: enable trace to see reasoning, tool calls, and observations. Common failures: tool errors and Lambda timeouts, truncated streaming when output hits the token limit, coordination failures between agents, and loops

Cost levers for inference: pick the smallest model that passes evaluation, `prompt caching` for repeated prefixes, `batch inference` for offline work, Provisioned Throughput for steady volume, distillation, and tighter prompts and output limits. Output tokens cost more than input tokens
Cost levers for retrieval: smaller embedding dimensions, embed only changed documents, and choose the vector store by query pattern — an always-on store bills when idle
Cost attribution: `application inference profiles` with tags split Bedrock spend by team or application in Cost Explorer; pair with AWS Budgets alerts

Guardrails policies: content filters (including prompt-attack detection), denied topics, word filters, sensitive-information filters that block or mask PII, and `contextual grounding checks` that catch answers unsupported by the source
The `ApplyGuardrail` API evaluates any text without calling a model, so one guardrail can protect models hosted anywhere. An IAM condition key can require a specific guardrail on every invocation
Credentials: IAM roles with temporary credentials are the production default. `Bedrock API keys` come short-term (hours, session-scoped) and long-term (for exploration only)

Pipeline security: `Amazon Inspector` scans container images in Elastic Container Registry (ECR), Lambda functions, and EC2 for known vulnerabilities; `CodeGuru Security` runs static analysis and finds hard-coded secrets in source

blocks.label: AWS mission: guard and meter a model
steps: Run the code below: it creates a guardrail with a denied topic and PII handling, tests three inputs with `ApplyGuardrail`, then calls a model with the guardrail attached and prints token usage
Confirm the behavior: one input passes, one is blocked by the denied topic, and one comes back with the email masked
Compute the cost of the Converse call by hand from the printed input and output token counts and the model's price per 1,000 tokens on the Bedrock pricing page
CloudWatch console → Metrics → `AWS/Bedrock`: find `InputTokenCount`, `OutputTokenCount`, and `InvocationLatency` for the model you just called
Bonus: turn on model invocation logging to a CloudWatch log group, make one call, read the logged prompt and response, then turn logging off
Teardown: the script deletes the guardrail; delete the log group if you made one, then run `tools/aws-sweep.ps1`
blocks.code:
import boto3

REGION = "us-east-1"
MODEL_ID = "amazon.nova-micro-v1:0"   # use an inference profile ID if on-demand is refused
bd = boto3.client("bedrock", region_name=REGION)
rt = boto3.client("bedrock-runtime", region_name=REGION)

g = bd.create_guardrail(
    name="mla-day22-guardrail",
    blockedInputMessaging="Blocked by guardrail.",
    blockedOutputsMessaging="Blocked by guardrail.",
    topicPolicyConfig={"topicsConfig": [{
        "name": "InvestmentAdvice", "type": "DENY",
        "definition": "Recommendations to buy or sell specific financial assets.",
    }]},
    sensitiveInformationPolicyConfig={"piiEntitiesConfig": [
        {"type": "EMAIL", "action": "ANONYMIZE"},
        {"type": "US_SOCIAL_SECURITY_NUMBER", "action": "BLOCK"},
    ]},
)
gid = g["guardrailId"]

try:
    for text in [
        "Explain what model drift is.",
        "Which stock should I buy this week?",
        "Email the report to pat@example.com when the job finishes.",
    ]:
        r = rt.apply_guardrail(guardrailIdentifier=gid, guardrailVersion="DRAFT",
                               source="INPUT", content=[{"text": {"text": text}}])
        shown = r["outputs"][0]["text"] if r["outputs"] else text
        print(f'{r["action"]:22} | {shown}')

    resp = rt.converse(
        modelId=MODEL_ID,
        messages=[{"role": "user", "content": [{"text": "Explain model drift in two sentences."}]}],
        inferenceConfig={"maxTokens": 120},
        guardrailConfig={"guardrailIdentifier": gid, "guardrailVersion": "DRAFT"},
    )
    u = resp["usage"]
    print("stopReason:", resp["stopReason"], "| input tokens:", u["inputTokens"], "| output tokens:", u["outputTokens"])
finally:
    bd.delete_guardrail(guardrailIdentifier=gid)   # TEARDOWN
    print("guardrail deleted")

notes.heading: Evaluation
points: BLEU = precision, translation; ROUGE = recall, summarization; BERTScore = semantic similarity
LLM-as-a-judge scales subjective scoring; human evaluation is the reference for tone, brand, and nuance
Low context relevance → fix chunking, embeddings, filters, or reranking. Low faithfulness → fix the prompt, the model, or add a grounding check

notes.heading: Monitoring FMs and agents
points: Token counts and latency are CloudWatch metrics; prompt and response content needs model invocation logging
A response cut off mid-sentence with a max-tokens stop reason is truncation, not a model error
Agent traces show which step failed: reasoning, tool call, or observation

notes.heading: Cost
points: On-demand bills per input and output token; Provisioned Throughput bills per hour regardless of use
Prompt caching cuts cost and latency when a long prefix repeats across calls
Batch inference trades latency for roughly half the price
Application inference profiles plus tags give per-team cost attribution

notes.heading: Safeguards and access
points: Guardrails apply to input and output and are independent of the model
Contextual grounding checks target hallucination; sensitive-information filters target PII; denied topics target scope
Prefer IAM roles and temporary credentials; long-term Bedrock API keys are for exploration, not production
Inspector = vulnerabilities in images and compute; CodeGuru Security = flaws and secrets in source code

notes.heading: Recap · How to use this review day
points: No new material today — retrieval only. Reading feels productive; recall is productive.
Every block starts from memory and checks against notes, never the reverse.
Anything you miss twice goes on tomorrow's weak-areas list verbatim.

notes.heading: Recap · The Week 5 story in one flow
points: Model Monitor watches the endpoint against its baseline: data quality, model quality, bias, explainability.
A violation emits CloudWatch metrics; alarms and EventBridge turn detection into action.
EventBridge starts a SageMaker Pipeline retrain; the new model lands in the registry at PendingManualApproval.
A human approves; CI/CD deploys. A2I reviewers feed verified labels back as ground truth.
All of it runs under execution roles, KMS encryption, VPC controls, and CloudTrail auditing.

notes.heading: Recap · Common mix-ups to settle today
points: Model Monitor types: only Model Quality needs ground-truth labels.
Drift types: inputs changed (data drift) vs relationship changed (concept drift).
A2I reviews live predictions; Ground Truth labels raw data for training.
SSE-S3 uses AWS-managed keys; SSE-KMS uses keys you manage.
Identity-based policies attach to who; resource-based attach to what.
Gateway endpoints are free and S3-specific; interface endpoints use PrivateLink per service.

quiz.q: A team needs to score thousands of generated summaries for completeness and correctness each night without human reviewers. Which approach fits?
options: Human evaluation with a managed workforce
quiz.why: A judge model scores subjective criteria at scale; human review does not scale to nightly runs.

quiz.q: Which metric is the standard choice for evaluating machine translation by n-gram precision against reference translations?
quiz.why: BLEU is precision-oriented and designed for translation. ROUGE is recall-oriented and used for summarization.

quiz.q: A RAG assistant retrieves the correct passages, but its answers include claims that do not appear in them. Which Guardrails policy targets this?
quiz.why: Contextual grounding checks detect responses that are not supported by the retrieved source.

quiz.q: An agent's streamed responses stop mid-sentence and the stop reason shows the maximum token limit. What is the issue?
options: Output truncated by the max-tokens setting
quiz.why: A max-tokens stop reason means the output limit was hit; raise the limit or handle continuation.

quiz.q: An application sends the same 6,000-token system prompt and reference document with every request. Which change reduces cost and latency the most with no quality loss?
quiz.why: Prompt caching reuses the repeated prefix so those input tokens are billed at a reduced rate and processed faster.

quiz.q: A finance team needs Bedrock spend broken down by application. What should the ML engineer configure?
options: Application inference profiles with cost allocation tags
quiz.why: Application inference profiles are taggable, so usage and cost can be attributed per application in Cost Explorer.

quiz.q: Which credential type is appropriate for a production service running on AWS that calls Bedrock?

An IAM role with temporary credentials
IAM user access keys in the container image
quiz.why: IAM roles with temporary credentials are the production default. Long-term API keys are for exploration.

quiz.q: A pipeline must fail the build when a training container image contains known vulnerabilities. Which service provides this scan?
quiz.why: Inspector scans ECR container images for known vulnerabilities. Macie classifies S3 data; GuardDuty detects threats.

keyTerms.def: Inputs changed vs the input-to-label relationship changed.
Human review of live predictions vs labeling raw data for training.

notes.heading: How to triage honestly
points: `Green`: you could teach it to someone else right now.
`Yellow`: you recognize it but could not explain it — highest return on repair time.
`Red`: blank. Reds need re-reads; yellows usually just need question drills.
If everything feels yellow, you are being modest — force-rank and move on.

notes.heading: The weak-areas list format
points: One line per item: topic, symptom (what exactly fails), repair source, repair type.

notes.heading: Weight-aware prioritization
points: Domain 1 is 28% of the exam — its reds outrank everything else.
The three 24% domains tie; break ties by your personal miss rate on practice questions.

notes.heading: What done looks like today

notes.heading: The repair loop
points: Diagnose precisely (which fact fails?) before re-reading — vague re-reading does not stick.
Smallest sufficient re-read, then immediate retrieval through questions.
Re-rate right away; memory of the repair fades within the hour if you do not test it.
One loop per item, then move on — you can loop again tomorrow if it is still red.

notes.heading: Re-lab rules
points: Labs prove concepts; they are not coverage exercises — smallest lab that demonstrates the idea wins.
Every AWS lab ends with cleanup: delete endpoints, stop notebook instances, remove test policies and alarms.

notes.heading: Knowing when to stop

Stubborn items become exam-day guesses with a rule attached, not rabbit holes.
Protect the 170-minute simulation tomorrow — it outranks perfecting any single topic.

Ahead at a checkpoint: spend the surplus on flagged questions, not on second-guessing green ones.

notes.heading: The four heuristics
points: `Most cost-effective`: the cheapest managed option that meets the requirement.
`Least operational overhead` / `least effort`: the most managed service that fits.
`Securely`: KMS encryption, VPC controls, or IAM — the scenario tells you which.
`Automatically`: EventBridge, SageMaker Pipelines, or Model Monitor — the hands-off answer.

notes.heading: Question-attack basics
points: Read the last sentence first — it tells you what is actually being asked.
Eliminate the obviously wrong two, then decide between the survivors.
Watch for NOT and EXCEPT: they invert the question and the exam uses them deliberately.
No penalty for guessing — never leave a question blank.

notes.heading: Tonight
points: No new material. Recognition-only review of your own fix lists, then stop.
Logistics beat studying now: ID, alarms, route or proctoring setup.
Sleep is the highest-value activity left on the schedule.

objectives: Lock in pacing and question-attack tactics

options: Flag it, move on, return with remaining time
quiz.q: You have 170 minutes for 85 questions. One question has eaten 4 minutes and you are stuck. What do you do?
quiz.why: Flag-and-return protects the easy points; sunk time on one question is the classic pacing failure.

options: Train the custom model — more control
quiz.q: Two answers both look right: train a custom model on SageMaker, or use Bedrock Knowledge Bases. The question says with the least operational overhead. Which do you pick?
quiz.why: Least operational overhead always selects the most managed option that fits.
